body.text: Beau Lamarre-Condon is a murderer. This is the evidence that convicted him
By his own admissions in court, Beau Lamarre-Condon has lied, deceived, gaslit, destroyed evidence, and treated the bodies of a Sydney couple in a terrible way.
The former police officer's trial hinged on a jury believing his version of events about what happened to Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024.
He is now, through a jury's verdict, a convicted double murderer.
A budding relationship
Within weeks of first meeting on New Year's Eve, Mr Baird and Mr Davies were smitten.
Mr Baird visited family in Victoria with Mr Davies in early 2024. Weeks later, he sent his mum a photo from a concert, announcing that he and the Qantas flight attendant were now boyfriends.
One of Mr Baird's close friends described them as "the real deal" and had never seen him happier.
Mr Baird, a former Channel 10 television presenter, was about to move house and start a new job that February.
But someone from his past had prompted him to tell relatives he was fearful and suspected he was being followed.
On February 19, 2024, that person — Lamarre-Condon — stood outside Mr Baird's Paddington share house dressed as an Uber Eats driver.
Not long after he entered the property, three gunshots echoed through the street.
Four days later, Lamarre-Condon walked into Bondi Beach Police Station and surrendered.
The bodies of Mr Baird and Mr Davies were found in a rural area south-west of Sydney the following week.
In the NSW Supreme Court, more than two and a half years later, prosecutors laid out allegations of intrusion, obsession, infatuation and stalking.
The Crown said this escalated to the planned murder of Mr Baird, and the murder of his new boyfriend, Mr Davies, because he was a witness to the crime.
Lamarre-Condon told the jury a different version from the witness box: that the shootings were acts of self-defence.
WARNING: This story contains details that readers may find confronting.
The agitated witness
When detectives first went to 60 Brown Street looking for Mr Baird, they found three cleaners who had been organised because he was moving out.
There was no sign of Mr Baird or Mr Davies, whose possessions had been discovered in a Cronulla skip bin by a bowls club grounds keeper.
Bloodied clothing and bedding heightened the concern and first raised an alarm.

In court, jurors were shown forensic evidence methodically documented at the house — a bullet hole in the kitchen floor and bedroom door, a ricochet mark on a kitchen wall, a fired cartridge above the kitchen cabinet, and a bullet in a sub-floor area beneath.

Crown Prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC said the prosecution alleged Lamarre-Condon used his service pistol to shoot Mr Baird twice in the kitchen, including a second shot delivered in "execution" style, before shooting Mr Davies through the bedroom door as he called emergency services for help.

Lamarre-Condon did not have to step into the witness box, but after choosing to do so, he spent eight days outlining his version of events and rebutting challenges of it during a lengthy cross-examination.
Sporting a close-cropped haircut and clasping rosary beads, he spoke confidently and quickly.
His answers to sometimes narrow questions were often lengthy.
Lamarre-Condon appeared to be a defendant with deep knowledge of the brief of evidence, sometimes reciting documents or dates to support his own account.
His responses were occasionally accompanied by a smirk and inferred an understanding of the legal mechanics that precede a trial.

At various points during his testimony, he complained that the prosecution had "hidden" witnesses, accused the prosecutor of putting words in his mouth and said he believed he was being misled by a question.
The forensic evidence
To illustrate motive, the Crown alleged there was "an obsessive and jealous infatuation" with Mr Baird following their brief involvement the year before, which included two apparent splits.
Lamarre-Condon insisted it was a romantic, non-exclusive relationship in the earlier part of that year and they remained in contact.
In Lamarre-Condon's account of the day of the shootings, he went to Mr Baird's home to retrieve possessions, including a surfboard, a $25,000 Cartier ring and expensive clothing.
He said he wanted to ensure nobody was home to avoid allegations of harassment or the possibility of an AVO.

Mr Baird requested no further contact in November 2023, the jury heard, so after seeing an unattended delivery rider motorcycle, Lamarre-Condon said he put on the outfit, including a helmet, as a contingency plan in case Mr Baird was home.
He said he came across Mr Baird in the kitchen holding a knife and masking tape, packing a storage box, and claimed he "lunged" at him after yelling about being robbed.
Lamarre-Condon claimed he shouted "it's Beau" through the helmet, but during a struggle over the knife, aimed and shot at Mr Baird's shoulder to disarm him.
"I was 110 per cent going to have the knife in my throat and I would be dead … and Jesse Baird would be here instead."

He testified that after being shot the first time, Mr Baird grabbed the front of the gun with "all his might", before the two fell to the floor and Lamarre-Condon accidentally fired another shot, which hit Mr Baird in the temple.
"I've said from the start I am guilty of manslaughter and I'm responsible for his death, but it wasn't intentional," he told the jury.
The gun went "flying into the living room", where he said Mr Davies must have picked it up.
In the hallway, he said there was a second confrontation in which he attempted to show Mr Davies he was not a threat, but claimed his police training kicked in.
Trying to pivot the gun away from him, Lamarre-Condon said Mr Davies put his finger on the trigger and the gun went off, fatally striking him in the head.
Lamarre-Condon did not deny he made efforts to clean the scene, placed the men's bodies in surfboard bags and returned to the property later to transport them in a hired van.

The jury heard evidence about his contact with colleagues and friends both before this day and after, during what the Crown characterised as "a deliberate and calculated series of actions" to cover up his involvement.
Killer says he faced a 'moral dilemma'

In hours of CCTV footage played during the trial, Lamarre-Condon was shown going to ATMs, driving his Tesla or another vehicle hired in his mother's name, driving a van used to transport the bodies and making multiple stops at Bunnings stores.
His purchases across multiple days included cleaning supplies, coveralls, dust masks, cable ties, a wheelbarrow and bags of concrete.
He did not dispute that while a female friend was in the hire van, he drove the bodies of Mr Baird and Mr Davies to a farm in Bungonia and attempted, unsuccessfully, to sink them in a dam.
The bodies of the two men were ultimately left at the fence line of a Greek monastery in the Bungonia area.

Lamarre-Condon told the jury he faced a "moral dilemma" in deciding whether to go to police because if he went to jail for Mr Baird's manslaughter, he may be killed in prison "not because of who I am as a person, but because of the uniform I wear".
Mr Hatfield put to him, under cross-examination, that there was nothing moral about his dilemma and that he acted purely out of self-preservation.
He replied that was "not the case" and while he "did treat the bodies in a terrible way, but it wasn't entirely to save myself".
He admitted to sending messages from Mr Baird's phone to two housemates, a woman who had recently hired him and a friend of Mr Davies.
Lamarre-Condon also admitted he later threw the handset off a bridge in the Sutherland Shire, "essentially" to destroy potentially incriminating evidence.
While he accepted many of his actions following the deaths were "strategic", he denied the Crown's assertion that they were inconsistent with his account of manslaughter or an accidental shooting.

In a written statement, Mr Baird's brother confirmed there was no surfboard found in the tray of Mr Baird's ute when it was recovered two months after his death, despite Lamarre-Condon's claims in court that he had been searching for the vehicle expecting his board to be inside.
Answers for everything
Several friends or colleagues Lamarre-Condon had contact with in this timeline also gave evidence, including a younger male friend who was with him at a sports shop two days before the shooting.
Lamarre-Condon was recorded on CCTV purchasing a surfboard bag with cash.
"He said: 'Oh, can you stand next to this so I can measure it up against you?'" the friend testified.
In addition to his Bunnings purchases, he also bought another surfboard and two larger paddleboard bags, in which the men's bodies were later placed.

The Crown told jurors Lamarre-Condon had taken a series of preparatory steps in the lead-up to the murders, including firing his pistol in the Royal National Park, searching online for a silencer and asking police colleagues "peculiar" questions about investigative techniques.

But in response to many of these suggestions, Lamarre-Condon gave evidence about his deteriorating mental health at the time, saying he had been planning to die by suicide and wanted to spare someone from finding his body.
Mr Hatfield accused him of "exaggerating if not completely falsifying" evidence about being depressed to explain the apparent interest in firearms and to gain sympathy.
"That is not correct," Lamarre-Condon replied.
There was, it seemed throughout his cross-examination, an answer for everything.
He said he had a second SIM card delivered not to use as a "burner phone", as the Crown suggested, but to compile statements about workplace bullying.

His phone data showed deleted searches for hire cars not because he had individually erased the items, but because he may have been watching adult content and cleared the browser history more broadly.
Lamarre-Condon activated airplane mode on his phone not to conceal his location, but because he did not trust it during personal or sensitive conversations.
The hire car in his mother's name was booked because her vehicle was at a mechanic.
"You wouldn't bring a vehicle linked to your mum for a murder," Lamarre-Condon quipped to the Crown's suggestion that was part of the plan.
"No-one's saying it was a good plan, that's why you're sitting here," Mr Hatfield replied.
Baird 'petrified' about gun access

To help explore the previous connection between Lamarre-Condon and Mr Baird, the Crown tendered tranches of text message and social media communications, mostly where Lamarre-Condon was discussing Mr Baird with his confidants.
He denied the Crown's assertion he was obsessed from the beginning.

The jury saw a video he edited of the two on a farmstay weekend in March 2023, which the Crown said gave the false impression of an "idyllic relationship" when they were, in reality, "just casually seeing each other from time to time".

After they first cut ties in April that year, Mr Hatfield alleged Lamarre-Condon's obsessive behaviour escalated to stalking, including by tracking Mr Baird's location on Snapchat, engineering chance meetings and breaking into his home.

Lamarre-Condon denied he was a stalker and pleaded not guilty to a break and enter charge related to an August 2023 incident where Mr Baird chased what he thought was an intruder out of his bedroom one night.

Mr Baird firmly broke things off in mid-November 2023 after discovering Lamarre-Condon had gone through his phone, deleted messages with another man he was spending time with and blocked him, then lied about it.
He also become aware of a social media post by Lamarre-Condon, targeted at this perceived romantic rival, which falsely implied Mr Baird had sent him flowers.
During his five days of cross-examination, Lamarre-Condon accepted his response to being confronted by Mr Baird about the Instagram flowers lie could be regarded as gaslighting.
Beau Lamarre-Condon: Brett was in Melbourne ... last week and sent this to my mum with a cute note for her so I posted saying how cute this was as mentioned in the previous story?
Do you want to ask my mum? Wtf
What's weird about that??
I'm so confused why you're asking me that?
Jesse Baird: Can you send me the "previous" story?
Beau Lamarre-Condon: Well it's not on my story now so I can't. I'm so confused??? What is this about?
Jesse can you call me back this is f**ked
Mr Hatfield asked in cross-examination: "You lied to him and deceived him numerous times throughout your relationship?"
Lamarre-Condon: "On a number of occasions, yes."
Mr Baird discussed the situation with his former long-term partner, Corey-Dean Thorpe, who gave evidence Mr Baird sounded "petrified" and was worried about Lamarre-Condon's access to a gun.
His sister, Kourtnee Baird, said at the end of that year she noticed Mr Baird was fearful, scared, shaken up, and suspected Lamarre-Condon was following him.
Jury's decision

While much of Lamarre-Condon's defence relied on a jury accepting his word, the panel was presented with a substantial amount of forensic evidence that spoke for itself, along with an animated reconstruction of potential angles of the pistol.
A ballistics expert testified that the bullet hole in the kitchen floor was likely to have been from a shot at a nearly vertical angle.

The hole in the bedroom door was encircled by a speckled pattern known as "stippling", which jurors heard is caused by the particles propelled from a gun as a bullet is fired and can indicate the weapon was close to the surface.
A retired crime scene specialist officer observed what he believed was stippling around the wound to Mr Baird's temple.

In a video played to the jury, police fired a test shot from close range through the bedroom door — and the ballistics expert testified that it produced a similar hole and stippling effect when compared to the existing hole.

On Lamarre-Condon's version, the bullet that killed Mr Davies injured him first before getting stuck in the door, while on the Crown's case, the stippling was on the door because the door was between the barrel and Mr Davies on the other side.
In the days following the shooting, Lamarre-Condon spoke to friends and detectives about having an out-of-body experience during and after.
He initially maintained his legal right to silence when investigators were trying to find the couple's bodies.
Lead detective Sasha Pinazza recalled that after several days he was emotional and expressed a fear of being "judged", before indicating the Bungonia location on maps.
He implored that he was "not a bad person", the court heard.
This assistance came after he was urged to consider the state's "no body, no parole" legislation.
"The accused expressed a hope that he would one day be able to talk to Jesse and Luke's families," Detective Pinazza recorded in a written statement.
During the trial, members of those very families sat in the public gallery enduring what can only have been a torturous period observing the legal process.
In December last year, just over nine months before his trial, Lamarre-Condon was secretly recorded in custody during a visit with his male friend from the surfboard bag shop.
He suggested the friend had "misheard" an admission that he had in fact killed a "singular" person.
And he expressed confidence that a jury would believe his account that he "made a dumb decision" but did not go to the share house to hurt anybody.
The verdict can only mean they did not.
